Answer: Bridge closures and travel delays"},{"type":"text","text":"correct answer:"},{"type":"text","text":"blank 1 : Bridge closures and travel delays"},{"type":"text","text":"difficulty_level: Easy"},{"type":"text","text":"mark: 1"},{"type":"text","text":"Solution:"},{"type":"text","text":"Answer key: “The effect was sudden closures and dangerous delays.”

Audio script:
Hi, I’m Huy, a fourth-year civil engineering student. At the start, our capstone team visited a riverside town that floods every rainy season. The mayor asked for a low-cost way to predict bridge stress during storms so buses could be re-routed before damage happened. The cause was rising water and heavy trucks; the effect was sudden closures and dangerous delays.
Then, we drafted a plan: battery sensors on key beams, a solar trickle charger, and a dashboard for alerts. Our rule of thumb was cheap parts, clear data. In lab tests, the prototype behaved well. But during the first field night, we hit a snag—vibration from traffic masked the true load. As a result, the alert spiked even when water was low.
Later, we went back to square one on signal processing. We logged one week of “quiet” and “busy” periods, tagged by time and weather, and separated patterns. We added a median filter plus a rain gauge input; only when both load drifted and rain rose would the system warn. The box got heavier, but still portable. Costs crept up, so we swapped aluminum for recycled plastic and 3D-printed mounts. To keep everyone on the same page, we wrote a one-page checklist with icons for the maintenance crew.
By the next storm, the alerts matched reality: trucks slowed, buses used the detour, and the bridge stayed open longer. The town council gave us the green light to install four units along the corridor. Finally, in our debrief, we mapped every cause → effect → change: traffic noise → false alerts → filter; rain spikes → load drift → dual trigger; cracked mount → new material → stable housing. The biggest lesson? Engineering isn’t magic or guesswork; it’s careful notes, honest testing, and iteration that earns trust."}]
